newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Euro to be more dominant than mark, Bangemann says.
newsitem.headline: Euro to be more dominant than mark, Bangemann says.

text.p: The EU's single currency will be able to play a more prominent role than any of the national currencies, including the German mark, European Union Industry Commissioner Martin Bangemann said on Wednesday.

Bangemann, one of Germany's two members on the Commission, said the euro could over time take up some functions in world markets that are now the dollar's domain, but that the U.S. currency would remain the world's leader for the time being.
"We don't feel that the euro will or can become a second reserve currency alongside the dollar," Bangemann told a news conference.
"But we do feel it has positive effects in relation to the dollar as compared with relations between the national currencies as we now have them and the dollar," he added.
For example, goods such as the European aircraft Airbus may be priced in the euro instead of the dollar, he said.
Bangemann said the euro, due to be launched in 1999, would be a stable currency.

"I do not pretend it will be more stable than the mark but it will be a stable currency and it will be based on a much broader basis so it can function in a way which is even more prominent and stronger than any national currency, including the D-mark," he said.
"The euro is stronger than any national currency so it can (over time) take up some functions which are now lost to the dollar," Bangemann said.
He also said that countries thaty stay outside the European Union's planned economic and monetary union will suffer economically.
"I personally believe that those who stay out will suffer from that," he said.
Bangemann said there would be no sudden exodus from London as a place to raise funds if Britain decided to stay out when monetary union is introduced in 1999.
But, the German commissioner added, "you will have a creeping effect which is negative."
For example, investors seeking security would feel safer in the euro-zone and the cost of capital would be lower.
"So there are all kinds of difficulties," Bangemann added.
If Britain decides to stay outside, the domestic debate would change in substance and tone, he said. "Those who are suffering from being out will start a debate (on) why shouldn't we now join."
Bangemann stressed that the Commission did not want to put pressure on any country to join the single currency.
